proxy_language: Proto-Afroasiatic (reconstructed, Semitic-leaning with Natufian-adjacent Levantine proxy)
proxy_rationale: The Geometric Kebaran (c. 14,500-12,500 BP, Levant and Sinai/Negev) is known only archaeologically (microlith assemblages, mobile foragers). No language can be linked to it. The most defensible, still very weak, proxy is the Proto-Afroasiatic/Proto-Semitic root layer sometimes associated by Ehret and Militarev with Natufian-era Levantine foragers; this is a hypothesis, not evidence. Alternative: Proto-Semitic as reconstructed by Kogan/Huehnergard. Names are best treated as invented words in a Semitic-looking triconsonantal style, flagged as speculative.
phonology: Proto-Semitic-style inventory (conventional reconstruction): stops b, t, d, k, g, q (emphatic uvular/velar), t. (emphatic), voiceless/voiced fricatives s, z, s. (emphatic), sh (/s/-like, written s with caron in scholarship), h, h. (pharyngeal fricative), x, gh (voiced velar/uvular), ' (glottal stop), ` (voiced pharyngeal), nasals m, n, liquids l, r, glides w, y. Vowels: short a, i, u and long a:, i:, u: (Proto-Semitic had three vowel qualities with length contrast). For game spelling a simplified set is recommended.
phonotactics: Syllables (C)V(C): CV, CVC, CV:C; no initial vowel (glottal stop fills onset); word-initial clusters avoided; medial CC only across syllable boundary (CVC.CV); word-final consonant common, final long vowels rare; geminates allowed medially (e.g. -bb-, -ll-). Roots are typically triconsonantal (CCC), also biconsonantal nominal roots (CVC) inherited from Afroasiatic. Stress not marked in spelling.
orthography: Use plain Latin scholarly transliteration with simplified digraphs: sh for /sh/, kh for /x/, gh for voiced velar/uvular fricative, th for interdental, dots/diacritics dropped (emphatics written as plain letters or with q); apostrophe for glottal stop, ` replaced by apostrophe-free 'a'. Long vowels written doubled (aa, ii, uu) or with macron.
morphology: Root-and-pattern (templatic) morphology: consonantal root interleaved with vowel patterns (CaCaC, CiCC, CuCC, maCCaC for place, miCCaC for instrument). Gender: masculine unmarked, feminine -at (or -a / -t). Dual -aan / -ayn and plural -uu/-uuna, -aat. Prefixes: ma- (place/instrument), ta- (abstract/reflexive), sa-/sha- (causative). Suffix -y for relational adjective. Definiteness and case endings (-u nominative, -i genitive, -a accusative) in the Proto-Semitic style; may be dropped in names.
compounding: Genitive (construct state): head noun first, dependent follows without article: 'X of Y' = X-Y (head + genitive noun), optionally with a linking -i / -u vowel (e.g. bayt-i + noun). 'Y-maker' = ma-/mu-CCiC participle form or head noun 'baal/baali' (owner/lord of) + noun. Adjectives follow nouns. True compounds of the English type are not native; use construct-state juxtaposition.
noun_phrase_order: Head noun first; genitive/possessor after head; adjective after noun and agrees in gender/number; demonstratives after noun; numerals before or after (before for low numbers in later Semitic).

worked_examples.name: Qarn Abn
worked_examples.gloss: qarn 'horn/point' (head) + abn 'stone' (genitive); microlith as stone point

worked_examples.name: Mashyad
worked_examples.gloss: ma- 'place' prefix + shayd 'hunt' (root sh-y-d) -> maCCaC place noun

sources: Kogan, Leonid. Genealogical Classification of Semitic: The Lexical Isoglosses (2015)
Huehnergard, John. Proto-Semitic and Proto-Akkadian, in The Semitic Languages (ed. Hasselbach-Naumann, 2019)
Militarev, Alexander. Starling database: Afrasian Etymology Database
Ehret, Christopher. Reconstructing Proto-Afroasiatic (Proto-Afrasian): Vowels, Tone, Consonants, and Vocabulary (1995)
Bar-Yosef, Ofer. The Natufian Culture in the Levant (1998)
Kaufman, Daniel. Archaeological perspectives on the origins of modern humans (1999)
notes: No Geometric Kebaran text, name, or linguistic evidence exists; the proxy is a deliberately flagged guess. Names should sound broadly Semitic-style with triconsonantal roots and construct-state genitives, but nothing here claims to reproduce an attested language. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since the proxy is not Goidelic. Keep the forms simple (CVC/CVCV), avoid overly specific attested Arabic/Hebrew words so names do not read as modern Semitic.
